payload.explanation_text:
A cell membrane surrounds a cell and controls what moves in and out, so it regulates exchange with the cell's surroundings. Its main building blocks are phospholipids. Each phospholipid is amphipathic, meaning it has two different parts: a hydrophilic (water-loving) head and hydrophobic (water-avoiding) fatty acid tails. Because of this, phospholipids in water arrange themselves into a bilayer, a double layer with the heads facing the water on both sides and the tails tucked inside. Each layer of the bilayer is called a leaflet.

Fatty acids are carbon chains. A saturated fatty acid has no carbon–carbon double bonds, so its tails are straight and pack closely together. An unsaturated fatty acid has one or more double bonds, which create bends in the tail. These bends get in the way of close packing and increase fluidity. Fluidity describes how freely the membrane's components can move. Several things affect fluidity: whether fatty acids are saturated, their chain length, temperature, and cholesterol.

Cholesterol acts as a fluidity buffer. It restrains movement when the membrane would otherwise be too fluid, and it helps prevent the membrane from stiffening when it is cold. This helps the membrane stay workable across a wider range of temperatures.

The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins, where the components can move sideways within the membrane. Singer and Nicolson proposed this model in 1972.

The two leaflets are not identical; their compositions differ. Lipids seldom move from one leaflet to the other on their own. Enzymes called flippases, floppases, and scramblases help this movement.

Finally, carbohydrate chains on the outer surface form the glycocalyx, or sugar coating. It helps cells recognize each other and distinguish self from non-self.

Let's revisit this from a different angle, focusing on the tails of membrane fatty acids and on cholesterol.

A fatty acid is a chain of carbon atoms. The key question is whether the chain has any carbon–carbon double bonds. Saturated tails have no carbon–carbon double bonds. Their chains are straight, so they pack closely together, like pencils stacked neatly in a box.

Unsaturated tails are different because they contain carbon–carbon double bonds. A double bond creates a bend, or kink, in the chain. These kinks are the reason unsaturated tails are the ones that bend. Because the bent tails cannot line up tightly, they hinder packing, so the membrane becomes more fluid.

Fluidity means how freely the components of the membrane can move. A membrane with more fluidity lets its parts move around more easily.

Cholesterol acts as a buffer for fluidity. When the membrane is very fluid, cholesterol restrains excessive movement. When it is cold, cholesterol helps prevent the membrane from stiffening. In this way, cholesterol keeps the membrane's fluidity within a steadier range.

payload.explanation_text:
Let's try this again from a different angle, starting with what a cell membrane is made of.

A cell membrane is built largely from fatty acids. A fatty acid is a chain of carbon atoms. The key question is how those chains are shaped, because their shape changes how the membrane behaves.

Think of the chains as straight or bent. In a saturated fatty acid, the chain has no carbon-carbon double bonds. Without them, the chain is straight, so the chains can lie close together, like neatly stacked sticks. This tight packing makes the membrane less fluid.

In an unsaturated fatty acid, the chain has one or more carbon-carbon double bonds. Each double bond creates a bend, like a kink in a bent straw. Bent chains don't pack together as tightly, which makes the membrane more fluid.

Now, what does fluidity mean? Fluidity describes how freely the membrane's components can move. A more fluid membrane lets its parts move around more easily.

Cholesterol acts as a buffer for fluidity, meaning it keeps fluidity from swinging too far in either direction. When the membrane becomes very fluid, cholesterol restrains excessive movement. When conditions are cold, cholesterol helps keep the membrane from becoming stiff. In other words, cholesterol keeps fluidity in a steadier range.

To summarize: double bonds in unsaturated fatty acid tails create kinks that loosen packing and increase fluidity, while saturated tails pack tightly. Cholesterol moderates fluidity by limiting excess movement and guarding against stiffening in the cold.

concepts.name: Saturated vs. unsaturated fatty acids
concepts.taught_summary: Saturated fatty acid tails lack carbon-carbon double bonds, so they are straight and pack closely. Double bonds in unsaturated tails create bends that hinder packing and increase membrane fluidity. Fluidity is how freely membrane components move.

concepts.name: Cholesterol as a fluidity buffer
concepts.taught_summary: Cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity: it restrains excessive movement when the membrane is very fluid and helps prevent the membrane from stiffening when cold.
